claim: Species with similar genetics, morphology, and behaviour tend to have similar connectome architecture.
source: Altogether, results suggest that species with similar genetics, morphology, and behaviour tend to have similar connectome architecture. In other words, variations in connectome architecture reflect phylogeny.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the statistical findings to draw this conclusion.

source: Altogether, results suggest that species with similar genetics, morphology, and behaviour tend to have similar connectome architecture. In other words, variations in connectome architecture reflect phylogeny.

claim: The difference between intra- and inter-order topological distances is larger when only local (node-level) features are included compared to when only global features are considered.
source: We find that the difference between intra- and inter-order topological distances tends to be larger when only local (node-level) features are included in the estimation of the topological distance (i.e. degree, clustering coefficient, betweenness, and closeness; Figure 3b and e) compared to when only global features are considered (i.e. characteristic path length, transitivity, and assortativity; Figure 3c and f).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from analysis of topological features shown in Figure 3.

claim: Differentiation of orders is better explained by differences in local network topology than by global network topology.
source: These results suggest that differentiation of orders is better explained by differences in local network topology; conversely, global network topology appears to be conserved across species.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the topological distance findings to draw this conclusion.

claim: Global network topology appears to be conserved across species.
source: These results suggest that differentiation of orders is better explained by differences in local network topology; conversely, global network topology appears to be conserved across species.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the topological distance findings to draw this conclusion.

claim: The relative local connectivity of the anterior and the posterior ends of the cortex changes across taxonomic orders.
source: An illustration of this principle is depicted in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing that the relative local connectivity of the anterior and the posterior ends of the cortex changes across taxonomic orders (Barrett et al., 2020; Krubitzer and Kaas, 2005; Krubitzer and Kahn, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript references Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and cites supporting literature.

claim: The difference between intra- and inter-order topological distances is greater for binary than for weighted features.
source: We also observe that that the difference between intra- and inter-order topological distances is greater for binary than for weighted features (Figure 3a–c and d–f, respectively), independently of being local or global.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The strength of the connections is less important than the binary architecture of the connectivity matrix for differentiating taxonomic orders.
source: This suggests that the strength of the connections is less important than the binary architecture of the connectivity matrix.

claim: Network density varies across taxonomic orders.
source: Some of the features used for the estimation of the topological distance depend on network density, which varies across taxonomic orders (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

claim: Differences between intra- and inter-order topological distances are not driven by differences in network density.
source: Results, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6, suggest that differences between intra- and inter-order topological distances are not driven by differences in network density, but variations in wiring patterns, as captured by topological features, play a role in the observed phylogenetic variations in connectome organization.
evidence: The manuscript reports results after controlling for network density.

claim: Variations in wiring patterns, as captured by topological features, play a role in the observed phylogenetic variations in connectome organization.

claim: All connectomes display high and diverse levels of small-worldness.
source: Consistent with previous reports in individual species' connectomes (Hilgetag and Kaiser, 2004; Sporns and Zwi, 2004; Bassett and Bullmore, 2006), we find that all connectomes display high and diverse levels of small-worldness, suggesting that simultaneously highly segregated and integrated networks is a global trait conserved across mammalian brains.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings on small-worldness and cites supporting literature.

source: Consistent with previous reports in individual species' connectomes (Hilgetag and Kaiser, 2004; Sporns and Zwi, 2004; Bassett and Bullmore, 2006), we find that all connectomes display high and diverse levels of small-worldness, suggesting that simultaneously highly segregated and integrated networks is a global trait conserved across mammalian brains.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the small-worldness findings.

source: Specifically, species that are part of the same taxonomic order tend to display similar connectome architecture, suggesting that brain network organization is under selection pressure (see also Butler and King, 2004; Lande, 1976; Wright, 1931 for an alternative mechanism of trait evolution characterized by pure drift models based on Brownian motion), analogous to size, weight, or colour.

claim: A uniform parcellation scheme (200 nodes) was implemented to facilitate comparison of network architecture across species.
source: Even though the sizes of the regions differ across species, we opted for a uniform parcellation scheme (i.e. 200 nodes) for several reasons. First, to our knowledge, there is no MRI parcellation for the brains of the majority of the species studied here. Second, how brain regions correspond to one another across species (i.e. homologues) is still not completely understood for many regions and for many species. Third, comparing networks of different sizes introduces numerous analytical biases because most network measures trivially depend on size, making the comparison challenging.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly justifies the uniform parcellation approach.
